name: Inca Empire
era: About 1438 to 1572, and a living Andean world
line: Give and receive in turn, work with your hands and thank the earth.

quote.text: Today for you, tomorrow for me.
quote.source: Kunan qampaq, paqarin ñoqapaq. The rule of ayni, the exchange of help between households

quotes.text: Do not steal, do not lie, do not be lazy.
quotes.source: Ama sua, ama llulla, ama qhella. Traditionally ascribed to the Incas and first written down under Spanish rule

quotes.text: Envy is a worm that gnaws and consumes the entrails of the envious.
quotes.source: Garcilaso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries of the Incas, 1609, book 6, trans. Harold V. Livermore

quotes.text: What rainbow is this black rainbow that rises?
quotes.source: Apu Inka Atawallpaman, on the death of Atahualpa, 16th century, after the Spanish version of José María Arguedas

quotes.text: To write it is to weep.
quotes.source: The First New Chronicle and Good Government, 1615. Translated from the Spanish

quotes.text: I believe that, in human memory, there has been no account of a road as great as this.
quotes.source: Chronicle of Peru, 1553, on the Inca highway. Translated from the Spanish

quotes.text: I will return, and I will be millions.
quotes.source: The Aymara leader’s last words before his execution in 1781, as handed down

words.usage: The Incas’ name for their realm: four quarters meeting at Cusco.
The capital, laid out in the shape of a puma. The name is often explained as navel.
The ruler, held to be the son of the Sun. Inca first meant the ruling lineage, not the whole people.
The ruler’s principal wife, daughter of the Moon, with her own lands and authority.
The divine ancestor of the Inca house. His main temple, the Qorikancha, was sheeted in gold.

words.meaning: Mother Earth; mother of time and space
words.usage: The living earth who feeds and must be fed. Still honoured across the Andes with the first drops of every drink.
The great snow peaks are persons who watch over the valleys beneath them.
A spring, a rock, a mummy, a twin ear of maize: anything in which unusual power shows itself.
One word for space and time together. An age of the world, and the turning over that ends it.
A group of families who hold land in common, share an ancestor and owe one another labour.
Help given that must be returned in kind: a day’s ploughing for a day’s ploughing. It extends to the earth and the mountains.
The whole community turns out for a job that benefits all, such as cleaning the canals, and the sponsor provides food, drink and music.
Labour owed to the state in rotation: building roads, farming the Sun’s fields, serving in the army. The Incas taxed in work, not goods.
The hereditary head of an ayllu or province, who organised labour and was responsible for his people’s welfare.
Coloured strings with knots that recorded numbers in a decimal system, and perhaps narratives too. The Incas had no writing as we know it.
An official trained to make and read khipus. Each village had several.
Some forty thousand kilometres of paved and stepped roads binding the empire from Colombia to Chile.
Runners stationed in pairs every few kilometres carried messages and khipus about 240 kilometres in a day.
Lodgings and stores set a day’s walk apart along the roads.
Stone silos on windy hillsides, filled with freeze-dried potatoes, maize, cloth and weapons against bad years.
A cross with three steps on each arm, an Andean emblem of the levels of the world. Also the name of the Southern Cross.
Two different things that belong together and complete each other, like two hands or a married couple.
Every community, and Cusco itself, was divided into two halves that competed and cooperated.
The Quechua language, spread by the Incas as a common tongue and spoken today by some eight to ten million people.
Called chicha in Spanish. Brewed by women, offered to the Sun and the dead, and owed by every host to those who work for him.
A few drops poured on the ground for Pachamama before one drinks.
Potatoes left out in the frost, trodden to squeeze out the water and dried in the sun. They keep for years.
Tapestry woven of alpaca and vicuña by specialists. Cloth was the most valued thing in the Inca world, above gold.

words.meaning: An ancestor; a mummy; a young tree
words.usage: The preserved bodies of the dead rulers were dressed, fed and consulted, and kept their own estates.
The river of the sky. The Andean constellations are the dark shapes in it: a llama, a toad, a serpent, a fox.

practices.name: Greet the sun, thank the earth
practices.instructions: At sunrise go outside and face east. Stand until the sun clears the horizon or the rooftops, and greet it. Take the first drink of your day with you. Before you taste it, tip a few drops on to the ground, and say thank you to the earth for the food you will eat today. Then drink. Look at the nearest hill or high point and acknowledge that too.
practices.why: The Inca state centred on the Sun, whose rising at the solstices was watched from stone pillars above Cusco. The offering of the first drops, the ch’alla, is older than the Incas and is made today by millions of Andean people before any drink.
variations: On 1 August, the day of Pachamama, give the earth a proper share of a meal.
Learn where the sun rises at midsummer and midwinter from your home.
Pour the drops before every drink for one whole day.

practices.name: Ayni
practices.instructions: Do a piece of real work for someone today on the understanding that it will come back. Help a neighbour move, dig, paint, harvest, mind children, fix something. Make it labour, not money. Then keep the account honestly: write down what you have given and what you have received this month, and from whom. Where you are in debt, set a day to repay it in kind.
practices.why: Ayni is the rule under all Andean life. A household cannot plough, roof a house or bring in a harvest alone, so help is lent and returned, day for day. Those who receive and do not give back lose their standing. The same rule governs dealings with the earth and the mountains.
variations: Ask for help with something, and so open an exchange.
Return a favour that is years old.
Bring food and drink for everyone you work beside.

practices.name: Knot the day
practices.instructions: Keep today’s record on a string. Take a main cord and tie hanging strings to it, one for each thing you want to count: tasks done, people helped, hours worked, money spent, debts owed. Use a different colour for each if you can. Tie one simple knot for each unit, and a long knot of several turns for the numbers two to nine. At the end of the week read the cord back without notes.
practices.why: The Incas ran an empire of ten million people without writing. Census, tribute, storehouse contents and calendars were kept on khipus by trained cord keepers, who could recite them years later. About a thousand survive, and scholars can read the numbers.
variations: Record a whole week on one khipu.
Use position on the string for tens and hundreds, as the Incas did.
Tie one cord for what you owe and one for what you are owed.

practices.name: Walk the road
practices.instructions: Walk for forty-five minutes on foot, uphill for as much of it as you can find, at a steady pace that lets you breathe through your nose. Carry something for someone: a parcel to deliver, shopping for a neighbour, a message to give in person. Take steps and steep paths in preference to flat ones. When you reach a high point, stop, add a stone to a pile if there is one, and look back along the way you came.
practices.why: The Inca road system crossed the highest inhabited mountains on earth with stairways, causeways and grass suspension bridges. Everything moved along it on foot or on llamas. Travellers still add a stone to the cairns called apachetas at each pass.
variations: Run a short relay with a friend, passing a spoken message exactly.
Walk to deliver something you would normally send.
Climb the highest ground within reach and name what you can see.

practices.name: The three laws and the river of stars
practices.instructions: At the end of the day ask yourself three questions and answer them aloud. Did I take anything today that was not mine: goods, credit, time? Did I say anything that was not true? Was I idle when there was work to do? Put right tomorrow whatever needs it. Then go outside. If the sky is dark, find the Milky Way and look for the dark shapes within it, not the bright stars.
practices.why: Ama sua, ama llulla, ama qhella is the best known moral rule of the Andes, and the United Nations adopted it in 2015 as a principle for honest public service. Andean astronomers saw their constellations in the dark clouds of the Milky Way, which they called the river.
variations: Add a fourth, as some do: do not be servile.
Greet someone tomorrow with the three laws, as a wish.
Learn to find the Southern Cross or, in the north, the Pleiades, which the Incas watched to forecast the harvest.

tasks.name: Look through Guaman Poma’s drawings of the twelve months of work
tasks.meta: Art · the Royal Library’s online facsimile

tasks.name: Read the capture of Atahualpa in an eyewitness account
Listen to Hanacpachap cussicuinin
tasks.meta: Listen · a hymn in Quechua printed in 1631

tasks.name: Cook potatoes three ways, and learn the name of each variety
Journal: what did you receive today, and what did you give back?
A state with no money and no hunger: at what price?
Take your turn at a job that everyone leaves to someone else
Mend or make something of cloth
tasks.meta: Cloth was worth more than gold

tasks.name: Put something by for a bad year
Taste a potato cooked very simply, with salt
Pour a few drops on the ground before you drink
Tie a knot in a string for each thing you finish today
Climb the stairs at a steady pace without stopping
tasks.meta: Road runners did hills all day

tasks.name: Look for the dark patches in the Milky Way if the sky is clear
tasks.meta: The Incas saw animals made of dark space

tasks.name: Eat a simple meal of potato or maize and thank the earth for it

rules.why: Help, food and labour are owed in return. Keep the exchange going and keep it even.
Take nothing that is not yours, including other people’s time and credit.
Speak what is so. A community run on spoken promises cannot afford false ones.
There is always work. Do your share, and take your turn at the common tasks.
Before you eat or drink, acknowledge where it came from.
In good years put something aside, for yourself and for others.

read.title: The First New Chronicle and Good Government
read.creator: Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala
read.why: A letter of nearly twelve hundred pages from an Andean nobleman to the king of Spain, describing Inca life and colonial abuse, with 398 full-page drawings. It lay unread in Copenhagen until 1908.

read.title: Royal Commentaries of the Incas
read.creator: Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, trans. Harold V. Livermore
read.why: The son of a conquistador and an Inca princess, writing in Spain in old age, sets down what his mother’s family told him. Idealised and indispensable.

read.title: The Conquest of the Incas
read.creator: John Hemming
read.why: The standard narrative of the invasion and the forty years of resistance, written from the documents and from the ground.

read.title: The Incas
read.creator: Terence N. D’Altroy
read.why: The best modern account of how the empire was built and run.

read.title: Deep Rivers
read.creator: José María Arguedas
read.why: A novel of a boy caught between the Spanish-speaking world of his father and the Quechua world that raised him, by Peru’s great bilingual writer.

read.title: The Huarochirí Manuscript
read.creator: Anonymous, trans. Frank Salomon and George Urioste
read.why: The only book-length text in Quechua from the colonial period: the gods, mountains and origins of one province, as its people told them.

watch.title: Wiñaypacha
watch.creator: Óscar Catacora
watch.why: An old couple wait for their son in a hut high in the Peruvian Andes. The first feature made wholly in Aymara. Slow, severe and tender.

watch.title: The Great Inca Rebellion
watch.creator: NOVA and National Geographic
watch.why: Archaeology at a cemetery outside Lima changes the story of how the conquest was won, and by whom.

watch.title: Retablo
watch.creator: Álvaro Delgado-Aparicio
watch.why: A boy in Ayacucho is apprenticed to his father, a maker of painted altar boxes. Spoken in Quechua.

watch.title: Secrets of Lost Empires: Inca
watch.creator: NOVA
watch.why: Villagers rebuild a grass suspension bridge in three days, as their ancestors have done every year for five centuries.

listen.title: Hanacpachap cussicuinin
listen.creator: Anonymous; published by Juan Pérez Bocanegra
listen.why: A processional hymn to the Virgin in Quechua, for four voices. The first polyphonic music printed in the Americas.

listen.title: Sikuri ensembles of Lake Titicaca
listen.creator: Community panpipe bands of Puno and the Bolivian altiplano
listen.why: Dozens of players with pipes and drums. The melody is split between pairs of instruments, so that no one can play it alone.

listen.title: Huaynos
listen.creator: Singers such as Pastorita Huaracina, or the guitarist Manuelcha Prado
listen.why: The song and dance of the highlands, in Quechua and Spanish, bright on the surface and sad underneath.

listen.title: El cóndor pasa
listen.creator: Daniel Alomía Robles
listen.why: An orchestral piece from a Peruvian musical play, built on melodies its composer collected in the mountains. Later borrowed around the world.

art.title: Machu Picchu
art.creator: Built for Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui
art.why: A royal estate on a ridge above the Urubamba, with temples, fountains and terraces cut and fitted into the rock. Never found by the Spanish.

art.title: The stone of twelve angles
art.creator: Inca masons
art.why: A single block in a palace wall on Hatun Rumiyoq street, Cusco, fitted to its neighbours on twelve sides without mortar. A knife blade will not go between them.

art.title: The all-tocapu tunic
art.creator: Inca weavers
art.why: A man’s tapestry tunic covered in small square designs, each different, which may have carried meaning. In the Dumbarton Oaks collection, Washington.

art.title: Miniature gold llama
art.creator: Inca goldsmiths
art.why: A hollow figure six centimetres high, of the kind left with offerings on mountain tops. In the British Museum. Almost all Inca goldwork was melted down in 1533.

eat.title: Native potatoes
eat.creator: Boiled in their skins, with a sauce of chilli and herbs
eat.why: The potato was domesticated in the Andes, where more than three thousand varieties are still grown, in every colour and shape.

eat.title: Quinoa soup
eat.creator: With potatoes, herbs and a little chilli
eat.why: The Incas called quinoa the mother grain. It grows where maize cannot.

eat.title: Pachamanca
eat.creator: Meat, potatoes, beans and maize baked in a pit on hot stones
eat.why: The earth oven. The food is buried and the ground itself does the cooking.

eat.title: Ch’uñu
eat.creator: Freeze-dried potato, soaked and cooked in a stew
eat.why: Light, almost everlasting, and the food that filled the storehouses and fed the armies.

drink.title: Chicha de jora
drink.creator: Beer of sprouted maize
drink.why: Cloudy, sour and mild. In Andean villages a red flag or a bunch of flowers on a pole outside a house means a fresh batch is ready.

drink.title: Chicha morada
drink.creator: Purple maize boiled with pineapple peel, cinnamon and cloves
drink.why: A sweet, deep purple drink without alcohol, served cold.

drink.title: Muña tea
drink.creator: An Andean mint steeped in hot water
drink.why: Drunk for the stomach and against the effects of altitude.

customs.title: The first drops
customs.creator: Ch’alla
customs.why: Before drinking, a little is poured or flicked on to the ground for Pachamama. Guests do the same.

customs.title: Rebuilding the bridge
customs.creator: Q’eswachaka, each June
customs.why: Four communities in Cusco twist grass into cables and re-weave a hanging bridge across the Apurímac in three days, then feast. The custom has not lapsed since Inca times.

customs.title: The first haircut
customs.creator: Rutuchikuy
customs.why: A small child’s hair is cut for the first time by relatives and godparents, who each give a present for every lock. It ties the child into a net of obligation.

customs.title: Coca among Andean people
customs.creator: A sacred leaf
customs.why: Three perfect leaves are held up and offered to the mountains before chewing, and leaves are exchanged as a greeting. It is central to Andean religion and not something for visitors to play at.

games.title: Pichqa
games.creator: Dice game · Andes
games.why: Named for the number five. A single die, often a truncated pyramid, was thrown for points. It was played at wakes as well as for amusement.

games.title: Taptana
games.creator: Board game · Andes
games.why: A hunt game on a marked board, with one piece as the puma against many as the llamas. Guaman Poma drew Atahualpa playing a board game in his captivity.

games.title: Sapo
games.creator: Tossing game · Peru
games.year: colonial, with an Inca legend attached
games.why: Players throw brass discs at a table of holes, aiming for the open mouth of a metal toad. The story says the Incas threw gold pieces to a sacred toad in Lake Titicaca.

festivals.title: Inti Raymi
festivals.creator: 24 June, at Cusco
festivals.why: The festival of the Sun at the southern winter solstice, banned by the Spanish in 1535 and re-created as a great public pageant in 1944.

festivals.title: Pachamama Day
festivals.creator: 1 August
festivals.why: The earth is opened and fed with food, drink and coca before the planting season. All of August belongs to her.

festivals.title: Qoyllur Rit’i
festivals.creator: Late May or early June, in the Sinakara valley
festivals.why: Tens of thousands of pilgrims climb to a sanctuary below a glacier at 4,700 metres, with dancers from every district. Andean and Catholic devotion joined.

festivals.title: The renewal of Q’eswachaka
festivals.creator: The second week of June, in Canas province
festivals.why: Four days of cable-twisting, bridge-weaving and celebration.

places.title: Machu Picchu
places.creator: Urubamba valley, Cusco, Peru
places.why: Reached by train and bus or on foot along the Inca Trail. Numbers are limited and tickets sell out months ahead. Go early and walk up to the Sun Gate.

places.title: Cusco: the Qorikancha and Sacsayhuamán
places.creator: Cusco, Peru
places.why: The curved wall of the Sun temple under a Spanish church, and above the city a fortress-temple of zigzag walls built from stones as big as houses.

places.title: Ollantaytambo
places.creator: Sacred Valley, Cusco, Peru
places.why: A town still lived in on its Inca street plan, with water running in the original channels, beneath a great unfinished temple.

places.title: Moray and the salt pans of Maras
places.creator: Sacred Valley, Cusco, Peru
places.why: Concentric terraces sunk into the earth like an amphitheatre, perhaps for testing crops, and thousands of small salt pools worked by local families since before the Incas.

places.title: Isla del Sol
places.creator: Lake Titicaca, Bolivia
places.why: The island where, in Inca belief, the Sun was born. Terraces, a sacred rock and a long walk at nearly four thousand metres.

places.title: Ingapirca
places.creator: Cañar, Ecuador
places.why: The best preserved Inca site in the north: an oval Sun temple of fitted stone on an older Cañari sacred place.

ethics.title: Reciprocity
ethics.text: Nothing is taken without return. This holds between people, and between people and the land.
ethics.practice: Return one thing today that you have been given: help, a meal, attention.

ethics.title: Honesty
ethics.text: No theft and no lies. Doors in Inca towns were said to have no locks.
ethics.practice: Give something back that you have kept too long.

ethics.title: Industry
ethics.text: Idleness was punished. Even the old and the very young had tasks suited to them.
ethics.practice: Do one useful thing before you sit down this evening.

ethics.title: Care for the weak
ethics.text: Widows, orphans and the sick were fed from the community’s and the state’s stores, and their fields were worked first.
ethics.practice: Do the work of someone who cannot do it today.

ethics.title: Respect for the land
ethics.text: Earth, water and mountains are living elders. One asks before taking.
ethics.practice: Before you use something from the natural world today, stop and acknowledge it.

ethics.title: Provision
ethics.text: A good ruler, and a good household, fills the storehouse before the famine.
ethics.practice: Set aside one thing today for a time of need.

philosophy.title: Ayni
philosophy.text: The world runs on exchange. To live well is to keep one’s exchanges in balance with neighbours, ancestors, earth and sky.
philosophy.practice: With whom are you out of balance?

philosophy.title: Yanantin
philosophy.text: Reality comes in complementary pairs: upper and lower, male and female, right and left. Difference is not opposition. Each half needs the other.
philosophy.practice: What is the other half of something you think you do alone?

philosophy.title: Pacha
philosophy.text: Time and place are one thing. The past lies in front of us, where it can be seen, and the future comes from behind.
philosophy.practice: Turn round. What is coming that you cannot see, and what past is in plain view?

philosophy.title: The living landscape
philosophy.text: Mountains, springs and stones are persons with whom one has relations. A place can be greeted, fed and offended.
philosophy.practice: What place has shaped you, and what do you owe it?

philosophy.title: Wealth as work
philosophy.text: The Incas had no markets and no money. Riches were people’s labour, and a lord’s greatness was how many he could feed.
philosophy.practice: Measure your wealth today in what others would do for you, and you for them.

philosophy.title: Order and its price
philosophy.text: No one starved, and no one chose their work, their home or sometimes their spouse. Whole peoples were moved to suit the state.
philosophy.practice: How much freedom would you trade for security?

philosophy.title: Memory without writing
philosophy.text: A civilisation can keep its accounts, laws and history in cords, songs and trained minds.
philosophy.practice: What do you know by heart?

philosophy.title: Still here
philosophy.text: Quechua speakers say kachkaniraqmi: I still am. Five centuries after the conquest the language, the fields and the offerings continue.
philosophy.practice: What in you has survived everything?

intro: The Inca Empire was the largest state ever formed in the Americas before the arrival of Europeans. At its height around 1525 it ran for more than four thousand kilometres along the Andes, from the south of present-day Colombia to the middle of Chile, and held perhaps ten or twelve million people who spoke dozens of languages. Its makers called it Tawantinsuyu, the four parts together. It was built in less than a century.

The Incas began as one of many small peoples in the valley of Cusco, at 3,400 metres. Their own histories said that around 1438 a neighbouring people attacked, the old ruler fled, and a younger son named Pachacuti rallied the defence, aided by stones that rose from the fields and fought as soldiers. Pachacuti, whose name means the one who turns the world over, rebuilt Cusco in fitted stone and began the conquests that his son and grandson carried to the limits of the Andean world.

They ruled a vertical land of deserts, terraced valleys, high grassland and cloud forest, and they did it without writing, money, markets, iron or the wheel. Their solution was labour. Every household owed turns of work to the state: farming the fields of the Sun and the ruler, building roads and terraces, weaving, soldiering. In return the state fed the workers, kept vast storehouses against famine, and feasted its subjects with maize beer on a lavish scale. The principle was the one on which every Andean village already ran, reciprocity, stretched to cover an empire. Records were kept on knotted cords. Messages went by relay runners along a road system of forty thousand kilometres.

The order was real and it was hard. Conquered peoples were resettled in their thousands, far from home, to break resistance and fill empty valleys. Chosen girls were taken from their families to weave and brew for the state, and some children were sacrificed on the mountain peaks. The Inca nobility lived in great luxury. Many subject peoples hated them, which the Spanish soon discovered.

In the 1520s an epidemic from the Old World, travelling ahead of the Europeans, killed the emperor Huayna Capac and his heir. Two sons fought a ruinous civil war. The winner, Atahualpa, was resting at Cajamarca in November 1532 when Francisco Pizarro arrived with 168 men, horses and guns. They seized him in an ambush, took a roomful of gold as ransom and then killed him. Aided by tens of thousands of Andean allies, the Spanish occupied Cusco. An Inca state held out in the forests of Vilcabamba until 1572.

The colonial century that followed killed most of the Andean population through disease, forced labour in the silver mines and the breaking of the old systems of provision. But the people did not vanish. Quechua is spoken by some eight to ten million people today, and Aymara by two million. The potato terraces are farmed, the first drops are still poured for the earth, and help is still lent and returned.

This Onda takes its practices from that continuing Andean way: greeting the sun and thanking the earth, the exchange of labour, a record kept in knots, a long walk uphill, and three old rules at night.
guide.origin: The valley of Cusco in the southern Peruvian Andes, and from there along the mountains from Colombia to central Chile
guide.era: The empire expanded from about 1438. The Spanish seized its ruler in 1532 and killed the last independent Inca in 1572

figures.name: Manco Capac and Mama Ocllo
figures.bio: The founding ancestors, brother and sister, who emerged from a cave or from Lake Titicaca and settled where a golden staff sank into the ground at Cusco.

figures.name: Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui
figures.bio: The ninth ruler by the traditional count and the true founder of the empire. He rebuilt Cusco, reorganised its religion and built Machu Picchu as his estate.

figures.name: Topa Inca Yupanqui
figures.bio: His son, the great conqueror, who took the coastal kingdom of Chimor and pushed the frontier into Ecuador and Chile.

figures.name: Huayna Capac
figures.bio: The last ruler of an undivided empire. He died in the north of a disease the Andes had never known.

figures.name: Atahualpa
figures.bio: Victor of the civil war. Captured at Cajamarca, he filled a room with gold for his freedom and was garrotted on 26 July 1533.

figures.name: Manco Inca
figures.bio: Crowned by the Spanish as a puppet, he escaped, besieged Cusco for ten months with a huge army and founded the free state of Vilcabamba.

figures.name: Túpac Amaru
figures.bio: The last Inca of Vilcabamba, captured and beheaded in the square of Cusco before a weeping crowd.

figures.name: Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala
figures.bio: An Andean nobleman and interpreter who spent decades walking Peru and writing his illustrated appeal to the king.

figures.name: Inca Garcilaso de la Vega
figures.bio: Born in Cusco to a Spanish captain and the princess Chimpu Ocllo. He left for Spain at twenty-one and became the first great writer of the Americas.

figures.name: Túpac Amaru II
figures.bio: José Gabriel Condorcanqui, a trader and local lord who claimed descent from the last Inca and led the largest rebellion in colonial Spanish America.

figures.name: Micaela Bastidas
figures.bio: His wife and the chief strategist of the rising, who managed its supplies and urged him to march on Cusco sooner. She was executed in front of him.

figures.name: José María Arguedas
figures.bio: Novelist and anthropologist, raised by Quechua-speaking servants, who gave the Andean world its voice in modern literature.

history.detail: A small farming people establish themselves in the valley, among older and larger neighbours. Great Andean states had risen and fallen before them for three thousand years.
After defeating the Chanka, he takes the fringed headband of rule and begins to transform a local chiefdom into an imperial state.
A royal retreat is built on a saddle between two peaks, with some two hundred buildings and a population of perhaps seven hundred and fifty.
Topa Inca and Huayna Capac extend the realm to its limits. Roads, way stations, storehouses and provincial capitals are built throughout.
A sickness, probably smallpox, spreads south from the Caribbean and kills the emperor, his designated heir and a large part of the population.
Huascar in Cusco and Atahualpa in Quito fight for the succession. Atahualpa’s generals win and massacre Huascar’s kin.
Atahualpa enters the square on a litter with thousands of unarmed attendants. The Spanish fire cannon, charge on horseback and take him alive. Several thousand Andeans die in two hours.
Some six tonnes of gold and twelve of silver are melted down. Atahualpa is tried and strangled in July. The Spanish enter Cusco in November.
Manco Inca besieges Cusco and nearly retakes it. Failing, he withdraws to the forests beyond Ollantaytambo.
Viceroy Francisco de Toledo sends an army to the last Inca capital. Túpac Amaru is brought to Cusco in chains and executed.
Toledo resettles Andean people into Spanish-style towns and turns the old labour turn into forced service in the silver mine of Potosí.
A rebellion spreads from Cusco to Bolivia and is put down with some hundred thousand dead. Quechua dress, theatre and the memory of the Incas are banned.
A local farmer leads the Yale lecturer Hiram Bingham up to ruins his neighbours had always known. Peruvians had visited and written their names there before him.
Inti Raymi is revived at Cusco. Quechua becomes an official language of Peru in 1975, and in 2014 six countries together place the Inca road on the World Heritage list.

concepts.detail: Households exchanged labour. The state took labour and gave back food, cloth, beer and security from its stores. Markets played almost no part in the highlands.
Every married man owed a period of work each year, organised in units of ten, a hundred and a thousand households. It built everything the Incas left.
An Andean group held fields at different altitudes, from hot valley to high pasture, so as to produce everything it needed. The empire did the same on a vast scale.
Knots and their positions give numbers in base ten. Colour, twist and the way strings are attached carried further meaning that is only partly understood.
A ruler’s palaces, lands and servants stayed with his mummy and his descendants. His successor inherited only the office and had to conquer an estate of his own.
Whole communities were moved hundreds of kilometres, loyal peoples into restless provinces and rebels into loyal ones. Perhaps a quarter of the population was shifted.
Forty-one imagined lines ran out from the Sun temple in Cusco, with 328 shrines along them, each cared for by a particular kin group on a particular day.
Girls selected at about ten, housed in convent-like compounds, who wove the finest cloth and brewed for the state. Some were given in marriage as rewards.
Springs, outcrops, peaks and ancestors’ bodies were all charged with power and tied to particular families. Conquered peoples’ shrines were brought to Cusco as honoured hostages.

facts.text: Inca masons fitted many-sided stones weighing over a hundred tonnes so tightly that their walls have ridden out five centuries of earthquakes.
The potato, the tomato’s cousin from the Andes, now feeds more people worldwide than any crop except maize, wheat and rice.
The words llama, puma, condor, quinoa, jerky and guano all come from Quechua.
Relay runners could bring fresh fish from the coast to the ruler in Cusco, over the mountains, in two days.
The Incas performed skull surgery with survival rates higher than those of field surgeons in the American Civil War.
Guaman Poma’s manuscript was found in the Royal Library of Denmark in 1908. No one knows how it got there.

sensitivity.note: The Inca state ended in the sixteenth century. The Andean way of life it drew on is that of millions of Quechua and Aymara people today. This Onda borrows everyday practices of reciprocity and thanks. It is written by outsiders and needs review by Andean readers.
requiredCaveats: Offerings to Pachamama and the mountains belong to a living religion. The simple pouring of the first drops is shared freely. Full offering ceremonies are the work of trained specialists and are not for imitation.
Coca leaf is sacred and lawful in the Andes and is a controlled substance elsewhere. It is described here and is not part of any practice.
The Inca Empire was itself a conquest state that moved populations by force and practised human sacrifice. Many Andean peoples fought against it.
Quechua and Aymara communities still face discrimination and poverty. If you visit, see that your money reaches them.
